also: since mention has been made of

terms.grammar: mentiō, mentiōnis f., with faciō, facere, fēcī, factum; what is mentioned in the genitive, or dē and the ablative
evidence: Cic. Att. 6.1.8: in quā nōn ejus mentiōnem faciās
Plaut. Most. 813: nōlī facere mentiōnem tē hās ēmisse
Traupman 43: Nōlī dē autumnō mentiōnem mihi facere
terms.comment: What is mentioned goes in the genitive (Epicūrī mentiōnem facis, Cic. Att. 14.20.5) or takes dē and the ablative; Plautus also has an accusative and infinitive. The person told takes cum: fac mentiōnem cum avonculō, “mention it to my uncle” (Plaut. Aul. 685). Passive: quoniam facta lituī mentiō est, “since the trumpet has been mentioned” (Gell. 5.8.8).

evidence: Cic. Amic. 71: nōn commemorāre quī contulit
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to make mention of something, to recount, relate”; of bringing a thing up in speech, often in some detail.

terms.grammar: verb, defective; the genitive, or dē and the ablative
evidence: Caes. BC 3.108.1 (Lewis & Short): Achillam, cujus suprā meminimus
Cic. Phil. 2.91: meministī ipse dē exsulibus
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “rare but class.” in this sense; usually “remember” (see remember).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.201: perquam breviter perstrīnxī atque attigī
terms.comment: In passing: in trānsitū attingere, after Quintilian’s quae librō quīntō leviter in trānsitū attigeram (7.3.27, quoted by Morgan–Owens).

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 6 (Lewis & Short): quem honōris causā nōminō
Traupman 103, 345: eum nōlō nōmināre, I don’t want to mention him by name

phrases.latin: nōlī facere mentiōnem tē hās ēmisse
phrases.english: don’t mention that you’ve bought the house

phrases.latin: flēns mihi meam fāmam commendāstī; quae epistula tua est in quā nōn ejus mentiōnem faciās?
phrases.english: In tears you begged me to look after my good name: is there a single letter of yours in which you don’t mention it?

phrases.latin: odiōsum sānē genus hominum officia exprobrantium; quae meminisse dēbet is in quem conlāta sunt, nōn commemorāre quī contulit
phrases.english: A tiresome sort, those who throw their favours in your face: the one who received them should remember them, the one who did them should not bring them up.
